title: Women in Love
description: Two sisters, two men and the search for a complete relationship, set against the industrial Midlands and the Alps.
plot_or_argument: Ursula Brangwen and her sister Gudrun are schoolteachers in the Midlands. Ursula falls in love with Rupert Birkin, a school inspector, and Gudrun with Gerald Crich, the industrialist's son. Their relationships work themselves out through a series of set pieces — the wedding, the boating party, the water-party drowning, the sculpture of the horse, the snow in the Alps — and end with Gerald's death in the snow and Birkin's insistence that he needs another man's love as well as a woman's.
narrative_structure: Thirty-one chapters in a loose episodic structure, with symbolic set pieces and a tragic conclusion.
principal_characters: Ursula Brangwen; Gudrun Brangwen; Rupert Birkin; Gerald Crich; Hermione Roddice; Loerke; Thomas Crich
literary_form: Novel (privately printed in New York, 1920; London 1921)
historical_context: The industrial Midlands before the First World War, the colliery and the mine-owner, the artistic colony of London, and the Alps of the end — Lawrence's own years in England, Germany and Switzerland.
literary_significance: Women in Love is the finest English novel of the period after Ulysses and Woolf's major work: it is the great novel of sexual love in English, its set pieces are among the most memorable in modern fiction, and its analysis of industrial civilisation and the will to power has never been surpassed.

title: Lady Chatterley's Lover
description: The gamekeeper and the lady: the most famous banned novel of the century and Lawrence's last major work.
plot_or_argument: Constance Chatterley, married to Sir Clifford, a paralysed mine-owner, begins an affair with Oliver Mellors, the gamekeeper on the estate. Through the affair she recovers her body and her sense of life, while Clifford becomes a machine-man of the industrial world; the novel ends with Mellors working on a farm and writing to her of their future.
narrative_structure: Nineteen chapters in the third-person, with the affair structured in fourteen numbered encounters; three versions exist.
principal_characters: Lady Constance Chatterley; Oliver Mellors; Sir Clifford Chatterley; Mrs Bolton; Hilda Reid; Michaelis
historical_context: The post-war English Midlands, the coal industry, the crippled aristocracy and the new class of the technically educated industrial manager; the censorship battles that kept the book out of Britain until 1960.
literary_significance: Lady Chatterley's Lover is the most famous banned novel of the century and the book that ended literary censorship in Britain: the 1960 Penguin trial, which acquitted it, was the decisive moment in the modern history of English publishing, and the novel itself is Lawrence's final statement about the body, the machine and the death of England.
bibliographical_notes: Written in three versions (1926–28); printed privately in Florence in 1928; banned in Britain and the United States until the Penguin trial of 1960.

title: Crome Yellow
description: Huxley's first novel: a country-house party and the wittiest satire of the twenties' intellectual world.
plot_or_argument: Denis Stone, a shy young poet, is invited to Crome, the country house of the eccentric Wimbush family, and spends a weekend among the guests — the novelist, the painter, the mystic and the scientist — in a comedy of talk, flirtation and intellectual display.
narrative_structure: A weekend chronicle in the house, with set-piece conversations.
principal_characters: Denis Stone; Mr Wimbush; Priscilla Wimbush; Anne Wimbush; Mary Bracegirdle; Mr Scogan
historical_context: The English country house of the 1920s, the Bloomsbury intellectual set, and the postwar generation's exhaustion.
literary_significance: Crome Yellow is Huxley's first novel and the wittiest satire of the twenties' intellectual world: it invented the Huxley novel of ideas, and its country-house party became the model for a whole genre of English comedy.

title: Point Counter Point
description: The great English novel of ideas of the twenties: a dozen characters in musical counterpoint around love, science and the failure of belief.
plot_or_argument: The novel alternates among a large cast — the novelist Philip Quarles, the scientist Lord Edward Tantamount, the sensualist Walter Bidlake, the fascist Spandrell, the painter Mark Rampion — and builds a contrapuntal argument about the life of the mind against the life of the body.
narrative_structure: Contrapuntal structure alternating among a large cast, with Quarles's notebook as commentary.
principal_characters: Philip Quarles; Mark Rampion; Lord Edward Tantamount; Walter Bidlake; Spandrell; Lucy Tantamount
historical_context: London in the 1920s, the intellectual set, the new science and the cult of the primitive, and the post-war loss of faith.
literary_significance: Point Counter Point is the finest English novel of ideas of the period: its contrapuntal construction and its argument about the life of the body made it the model for the twentieth-century novel of debate.

title: Brave New World
description: The most influential English dystopia: a World State of engineered happiness, and the savage who cannot live in it.
plot_or_argument: In the World State of AF 632, human beings are bred in hatcheries and conditioned into five castes; pain, art, religion and family have been abolished, and happiness is administered in doses of 'soma'. Bernard Marx and Lenina Crowne bring back John the Savage from New Mexico, and he cannot accept the engineered happiness of the new world and is destroyed by it.
narrative_structure: Eighteen chapters in three parts, from the World State to the Reservation and back.
principal_characters: Bernard Marx; Lenina Crowne; John the Savage; Linda; Mustapha Mond; Helmholtz Watson
historical_context: Fordism and mass production, the eugenics movement, the psychology of conditioning, the Soviet Five-Year Plans, and the hedonism of the late 1920s.
literary_significance: Brave New World is the most influential English dystopia and one of the permanent books of the century: it invented the vocabulary — soma, conditioning, the feelies, the castes — in which the debate about technology and happiness is still conducted.

title: Eyeless in Gaza
description: Huxley's most experimental novel: a life told in fragments, and the search for a mysticism that will hold.
plot_or_argument: The novel tells the life of Anthony Beavis in a collage of dated fragments, from his Edwardian childhood through the First World War, his affairs and his political disillusion to his discovery of a pacifist mysticism in Mexico.
narrative_structure: A collage of dated fragments over forty years, moving backwards and forwards.
principal_characters: Anthony Beavis; Helen Amberley; Mark Staithes; Brian Foxe; Joan Thursley; Dr Miller
historical_context: The First World War, the 1920s and 1930s, the rise of fascism, and Huxley's own turn toward pacifism and mysticism.
literary_significance: Eyeless in Gaza is Huxley's most experimental novel and the record of his turn from satire to mysticism: its fragmentary chronology made it the most formally ambitious English novel of ideas of the decade.

title: The Perennial Philosophy
description: Huxley's anthology of the mystical tradition: the 'perennial philosophy' common to every religion.
plot_or_argument: Huxley assembles passages from the Upanishads, the Buddhist scriptures, the Christian mystics, the Sufis and the Taoists, and connects them with a commentary arguing for a single metaphysical truth underlying all religions.
narrative_structure: An anthology of mystical texts with an extended commentary in chapters.
historical_context: The Second World War, Huxley's years in California, and his study of Vedanta with Gerald Heard and Swami Prabhavananda.
literary_significance: The Perennial Philosophy is Huxley's most influential work of ideas and the founding text of the modern comparative mysticism: it made the mystical tradition available to a general readership and shaped the spiritual culture of the postwar decades.

title: Decline and Fall
description: The greatest English comic novel of the period: a theology student is sent down from Oxford and descends through a series of catastrophes.
plot_or_argument: Paul Pennyfeather is sent down from Scone College for running through the quadrangle without his trousers and becomes a schoolmaster at Llanabba Castle, where he meets the monstrous Captain Grimes, the dilettante Prendergast and the beautiful Margot Beste-Chetwynde. He is engaged to Margot, imprisoned for her white-slave traffic, and returned to Oxford to study theology.
narrative_structure: Three parts (school, society, prison) with a circular return to the opening.
principal_characters: Paul Pennyfeather; Captain Grimes; Augustus Fagan; Prendergast; Margot Beste-Chetwynde; Philbrick
historical_context: The late 1920s: the Bright Young Things, the public school, the Welsh prep school, the prison system and the respectable criminality of the upper class.
literary_significance: Decline and Fall is the greatest English comic novel of the period and the book that made Waugh's name: its straight-faced absurdity and its circular plot invented the modern English comic novel.

title: Vile Bodies
description: The definitive novel of the Bright Young Things: a comic whirl of parties, gossip columns and the coming war.
plot_or_argument: Adam Fenwick-Symes loses his manuscript at customs, wins and loses a fortune on a horse, and drifts through the parties of the Bright Young Things — Nina Blount, Agatha Runcible, Miles Malpractice — in a novel that ends with a battlefield of the next war and the famous last line 'Oh, Nina, what a lot of parties'.
narrative_structure: A rapid episodic narrative with a race, a party and a battlefield ending.
principal_characters: Adam Fenwick-Symes; Nina Blount; Agatha Runcible; Miles Malpractice; Lottie Crump; Colonel Blount
historical_context: London in the late 1920s, the gossip columns, the Bright Young Things, the crash of 1929, and the new mass culture of the cinema and the tabloid.
literary_significance: Vile Bodies is the definitive novel of the Bright Young Things: its speed, its jokes and its sudden ending made it the most brilliant English comic novel of the twenties.

title: A Handful of Dust
description: Waugh's darkest novel: the end of a marriage and the collapse of a civilisation, ending in a South American jungle.
plot_or_argument: Tony Last, the owner of Hetton Abbey, is devoted to his house and his illusions; his wife Brenda takes a lover, and their divorce is engineered — until the death of their son destroys every calculation. Tony escapes to Brazil, is captured by a madman who keeps him to read Dickens aloud, and ends his life in the jungle.
narrative_structure: Five parts, from Hetton Abbey to London to the Brazilian jungle.
principal_characters: Tony Last; Brenda Last; John Beaver; John Andrew Last; Mrs Beaver; Todd
historical_context: The English country house between the wars, the London of the Bright Young Things, and the Amazonian exploration narratives of the 1920s.
literary_significance: A Handful of Dust is Waugh's darkest and most perfect novel: its movement from comedy to desolation and its portrait of the country house as a religion made it one of the great English novels of the period.

title: Scoop
description: The funniest English novel about journalism: a country columnist is sent to Africa as a war correspondent and gets the wrong man.
plot_or_argument: William Boot, the author of a nature column in the Daily Beast, is mistaken for the novelist John Boot and sent to the fictional African state of Ishmaelia to cover a war. He stumbles into a scoop, wins the girl and the reputation, and returns to England while the real correspondents fail.
narrative_structure: Five books, from London to Ishmaelia and back.
principal_characters: William Boot; John Boot; Lord Copper; Salter; Mrs Stitch; Katchen; Corker
historical_context: Fleet Street in the 1930s, the Abyssinian crisis of 1935 and Waugh's own experience as a correspondent in Ethiopia.
literary_significance: Scoop is the funniest English novel about journalism and one of the great comic novels of the century: its portrait of Fleet Street, its African republic and its innocent hero made it the permanent satire of the foreign correspondent.

title: Brideshead Revisited: The Sacred and Profane Memories of Captain Charles Ryder
description: The great English elegy for the Catholic aristocracy: Charles Ryder, the Flyte family and Brideshead Castle.
plot_or_argument: Charles Ryder, an officer in the Second World War, is billeted at Brideshead Castle and remembers his youth: his friendship with Sebastian Flyte at Oxford, his love for Sebastian's sister Julia, the decline of the Marquess of Marchmain and the family's Catholicism, and the slow return of grace that ends with the chapel lamp relit.
narrative_structure: Book One (Et in Arcadia Ego) and Book Two (A Twitch upon the Thread), framed by a wartime prologue and epilogue.
principal_characters: Charles Ryder; Sebastian Flyte; Julia Flyte; Lady Marchmain; Lord Marchmain; Cordelia Flyte; Anthony Blanche; Nanny Hawkins
historical_context: Oxford in the 1920s, the English Catholic aristocracy, the country house, the 1930s and the Second World War.
literary_significance: Brideshead Revisited is the period's great elegy for the English Catholic aristocracy and one of the most loved novels in English: its portrait of Oxford, of the great house and of the workings of grace made it the century's most popular Catholic novel.

title: Sword of Honour
description: Waugh's finest novel: Guy Crouchback, the Second World War, and the comedy of honour.
plot_or_argument: The trilogy — Men at Arms (1952), Officers and Gentlemen (1955) and Unconditional Surrender (1961) — follows Guy Crouchback, a Catholic English gentleman, through the Second World War: the training camps, the Dakar expedition, Crete, Yugoslavia and the Italian peace, in a comedy of honour, incompetence and betrayal.
narrative_structure: Three volumes in a chronological war narrative.
principal_characters: Guy Crouchback; Apthorpe; Tommy Blackhouse; Virginia Troy; Uncle Peregrine; Ludovic
historical_context: The Second World War, the British army, the fall of Crete and the Yugoslav partisans, and the peace settlements of 1945.
literary_significance: Sword of Honour is Waugh's finest novel and the finest English novel of the Second World War: its comedy, its portrait of Guy Crouchback and its treatment of honour and faith made it the summit of Waugh's art.

title: The Mysterious Affair at Styles
description: The first Hercule Poirot novel and the founding book of the Golden Age: a poisoning at an English country house.
plot_or_argument: At the country house of Styles, the wealthy Emily Inglethorp is poisoned with strychnine; her new young husband, her stepsons and the household all have motives, and Hercule Poirot, a Belgian refugee, solves the case by the arrangement of the furniture and the broken coffee cup.
narrative_structure: A first-person narrative by Hastings, with the final explanation by Poirot.
principal_characters: Hercule Poirot; Captain Hastings; Emily Inglethorp; Alfred Inglethorp; John Cavendish; Lawrence Cavendish; Evelyn Howard
historical_context: The English country house of 1917, the Belgian refugee community, and the new detective fiction of the period.
literary_significance: The Mysterious Affair at Styles introduced Hercule Poirot and founded the Golden Age detective novel: it established the fair-play plot, the country-house setting and the eccentric detective, and it began the most successful career in the history of crime fiction.

title: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd
description: The most audacious solution in detective fiction: a murder in a village, and a narrator who is not what he seems.
plot_or_argument: Roger Ackroyd is found stabbed in his study in the village of King's Abbot, and Hercule Poirot, retired and growing marrows, is drawn into the case. The solution — that the narrator, Dr Sheppard, is the murderer — is the most famous coup in the genre.
narrative_structure: A first-person narrative by Dr Sheppard, with Poirot's final explanation.
principal_characters: Hercule Poirot; Dr Sheppard; Roger Ackroyd; Caroline Sheppard; Ralph Paton; Flora Ackroyd
historical_context: The English village of the 1920s, the country-house study and the small-town gossip network.
literary_significance: The Murder of Roger Ackroyd is the most audacious detective novel ever written: its solution changed the rules of the genre, and it remains the most famous example of the unreliable narrator in detective fiction.

title: Murder on the Orient Express
description: The most famous closed-circle mystery in the genre: a murder on a snowbound train and twelve passengers with a secret.
plot_or_argument: Hercule Poirot, travelling on the Orient Express from Istanbul, is snowbound in Yugoslavia when the American tycoon Ratchett is stabbed twelve times in his compartment; every passenger has an alibi, and Poirot's solution — that they all did it — is one of the most famous in detective fiction.
narrative_structure: A closed-circle investigation on a snowbound train, with Poirot's final reconstruction.
principal_characters: Hercule Poirot; Ratchett; Mrs Hubbard; Colonel Arbuthnot; Mary Debenham; Princess Dragomiroff; Greta Ohlsson
historical_context: The Orient Express of the 1930s, the Balkans, and the aftermath of a famous American kidnapping case.
literary_significance: Murder on the Orient Express is the most famous closed-circle mystery in the genre: its solution and its snowbound setting made it the definitive detective novel of the 1930s, and it remains the most widely adapted of all Christie's books.

title: And Then There Were None
description: The most perfectly constructed detective novel in English: ten strangers on an island, and a nursery rhyme that kills them.
plot_or_argument: Ten people, each guilty of a death the law could not punish, are lured to an island off the Devon coast by a mysterious host; they die one by one in the manner of the nursery rhyme 'Ten Little Soldier Boys', and the solution is revealed in a manuscript by the murderer, the judge Lawrence Wargrave.
narrative_structure: Ten victims in the order of the nursery rhyme, with a final manuscript explaining the plot.
principal_characters: Justice Wargrave; Vera Claythorne; Philip Lombard; Emily Brent; General Macarthur; Dr Armstrong; Mr Blore
historical_context: The Devon coast of the 1930s, the closed island setting, and the pre-war atmosphere of approaching catastrophe.
literary_significance: And Then There Were None is the most perfectly constructed detective novel in English: its mathematical elegance, its nursery-rhyme structure and its impossible solution made it Christie's masterpiece and the best-selling mystery novel of all time.

title: Whose Body?
description: The first Lord Peter Wimsey novel: a naked body in a Battersea bathroom and a missing financier.
plot_or_argument: A naked man's body is found in the bath of a Battersea architect, and Lord Peter Wimsey, the aristocratic amateur detective, investigates alongside Inspector Sugg and his manservant Bunter; the case turns on a missing financier, Sir Reuben Levy, and a substitution of bodies.
narrative_structure: An investigation in London, with Wimsey's reconstruction at the close.
principal_characters: Lord Peter Wimsey; Bunter; Inspector Sugg; Sir Reuben Levy; Mr Thipps; Mr Parker
historical_context: London in the early 1920s, the City and the art trade, and the postwar world of the aristocratic amateur.
literary_significance: Whose Body? introduced Lord Peter Wimsey and founded the English detective novel of character: its wit, its aristocratic detective and its fair-play plot made Sayers the finest writer of the Golden Age after Christie.

title: The Nine Tailors
description: The most perfectly constructed English detective novel: a body in a Fens churchyard and the bells of Fenchurch St Paul.
plot_or_argument: Lord Peter Wimsey, stranded in the Fenland village of Fenchurch St Paul on New Year's Eve, joins the bell-ringers in a nine-hour peal; a body is later found in a grave, and the solution turns on the ringing of the bells and an old crime of stolen emeralds.
narrative_structure: A village investigation structured around the nine-hour peal and the bell-ringing method.
principal_characters: Lord Peter Wimsey; the Rev. Theodore Venables; Hezekiah Lavender; Superintendent Blundell; William Thoday
historical_context: The Fenland village of the 1930s, the English campanology tradition, and the flood of the Fens.
literary_significance: The Nine Tailors is the most perfectly constructed English detective novel and Sayers's masterpiece: its use of the bells, its Fenland setting and its final flood made it the finest technical achievement of the Golden Age.

title: Gaudy Night
description: The first detective novel built on the inner life of a woman intellectual: Oxford, Harriet Vane and the poison-pen letters.
plot_or_argument: Harriet Vane returns to her Oxford college for the Gaudy and is drawn into a case of poison-pen letters and vandalism at Shrewsbury College; Lord Peter Wimsey arrives to help, and the novel becomes a study of the woman intellectual's place in the world as much as a mystery.
narrative_structure: A university investigation structured by the academic terms and the Gaudy.
principal_characters: Harriet Vane; Lord Peter Wimsey; the dons of Shrewsbury College; the Dean; Miss de Vine
historical_context: Oxford in the 1930s, the women's colleges, and the position of the educated woman in English society.
literary_significance: Gaudy Night is the first detective novel built on the inner life of a woman intellectual and Sayers's most personal book: its Oxford setting, its treatment of education and marriage made it a landmark in both detective fiction and English fiction of the period.
